strings.title: Times 10 and 100
strings.label: Day 1
strings.group: Grade 4 · Week 2 · Multiplying by One Digit
strings.strategy: Multiplying by 10 makes each digit worth 10 times as much (ones become tens); multiplying by 100 makes them worth 100 times as much.
strings.keywords: times 10, times 100, place value, ones become tens, groups of ten
strings.connection: Uses multiplication facts to 10 × 10. Sets up splitting by place value on Day 2.
watchFor: "Just add a zero" without knowing why: accept it, then ask "Why does a zero appear? What happened to the 6?"
Adding instead of multiplying (6 × 10 = 16): ask "Is that 6 groups of 10?"
Too many or too few zeros (24 × 100 = 240): ask "Is that 24 hundreds?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "What happens to a number when you multiply it by 10? By 100?" Land: each digit moves to a place worth 10 (or 100) times as much, so 6 ones become 6 tens.

problems.notes: Look for: 6 tens. Ask: "How many tens is that?" Word choice: "6 groups of 10 is 6 tens, 60." Model: ratio 1:6, 10:60

responses.tip: The target model. Ask: what happened to the 6?
Added. Ask: is that 6 groups of 10?

problems.notes: Look for: 6 hundreds. Ask: "How is this like the last one?" Model: ratio 1:6, 10:60, 100:600

responses.tip: Ask: is 60 the same as 6 hundreds?

problems.notes: Look for: 6 tens times 10 is 6 hundreds. Ask: "Why is it the same as the last one?" Model: text 60 x 10 = 6 x 10 x 10 ; = 6 x 100 = 600

responses.say: 60 is 6 tens. Ten of those is 6 hundreds.

responses.tip: x10 means 10 jumps of 60.

problems.notes: Look for: 24 tens, 240. Ask: "What happens to the 2 and the 4?" Model: ratio 1:24, 10:240

responses.say: 2 tens become 2 hundreds, 4 ones become 4 tens: 240.

responses.tip: Ask: is 2410 close to 24 tens?

problems.notes: Look for: 24 hundreds. Ask: "How can the last one help?" Model: ratio 1:24, 10:240, 100:2400

responses.tip: Ask: is that 24 hundreds or 24 tens?

problems.notes: Look for: 7 thousands. Ask: "What's the pattern?" Model: ratio 1:7, 10:70, 100:700, 1000:7000

responses.tip: Ask: how many zeros does 1000 have? Is that 7 thousands?

problems.notes: Look for: 3 × 4 = 12, so 3 × 40 is 12 tens. Ask: "Which fact helps?" Model: ratio 1:3, 4:12, 40:120

responses.tip: Added. Ask: is that 3 groups of 40?

strings.title: Split the Tens and Ones
strings.label: Day 2
strings.group: Grade 4 · Week 2 · Multiplying by One Digit
strings.strategy: Split the larger number into tens and ones, multiply each part, then add the parts.
strings.keywords: split, tens and ones, partial products, area model, add the parts
strings.connection: Day 1 multiplied tens. Today: tens and ones together. Like Week 1's split by place value, but multiplying.
watchFor: Writing the parts side by side (23 × 4 = 812): ask "Is 812 about 20 groups of 4?"
Multiplying only the tens (23 × 4 = 83): ask "Did the 3 get multiplied by 4 too?"
Losing track of the parts: write each product in its box on the area model.
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How did splitting the number help?" Land: split into tens and ones, multiply each part, then add. The area model shows both parts.

problems.notes: Look for: 2 × 4 = 8, so 8 tens. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: area 20 x 4
Look for: a known fact. Ask: "Hold on to this one too." Model: array 4 x 3
Look for: 80 + 12. Ask: "How do the first two help?" Word choice: "I split 23 into 20 and 3." Model: area 20+3 x 4

responses.tip: The target model. Ask: where are the 80 and the 12?

responses.say: I see it in the dots: 20 columns and 3 more.

responses.tip: Repeated addition. Ask: is there a quicker way?
Wrote the parts side by side. Ask: is 812 close to 20 groups of 4?

problems.notes: Look for: 90 + 18. Ask: "How will you split 36?" Model: area 30+6 x 3

responses.tip: Only multiplied the tens. Ask: did the 6 get multiplied by 3?

problems.notes: Look for: 200 + 35. Ask: "What are the two parts?" Model: area 40+7 x 5

responses.tip: A Day 4-style idea. Name it.
Wrote the parts side by side. Ask: is the answer closer to 200 or 2000?

problems.notes: Look for: 400 + 80 + 20. Ask: "Can you split a 3-digit number the same way?" Model: area 100+20+5 x 4

responses.tip: Friendly split. Name it.

problems.notes: Look for: 360 + 48. Ask: "Which facts do you need?" Model: area 60+8 x 6

responses.tip: Tomorrow's strategy. Name it.
Ask: should the answer be about 60 sixes, or a lot more?

strings.title: Over and Back
strings.label: Day 3
strings.group: Grade 4 · Week 2 · Multiplying by One Digit
strings.strategy: When a number is close to a ten, multiply the ten, then take away the extra group.
strings.keywords: friendly number, one group too many, take away a group, close to a ten
strings.connection: Like Week 1 Day 4 (add a friendly number, then take back the extra), but with groups.
watchFor: Taking away 1 instead of one group (39 × 4 = 159): ask "How many fours did you add too many?"
Adding the extra group instead of taking it away: ask "Did you make too many groups or too few?"
Not seeing the friendly number: ask "Is 39 close to a ten?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Why do we take away 4 and not 1?" Land: 40 × 4 is one group of 4 too many, so take away a whole group.

problems.notes: Look for: 4 × 4 = 16, so 16 tens. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: area 40 x 4
Look for: 160 − 4. Ask: "How is 39 × 4 different from 40 × 4?" Word choice: "39 fours is one four less than 40 fours." Model: area 40-1 x 4

responses.tip: The target strategy. Ask: what's in the strip we took away?

responses.say: The dots: 40 columns of 4, cross one out.

responses.tip: Splitting works too. Ask: which is quicker?
Took away 1, not one group. Ask: how many fours too many?

problems.notes: Look for: 3 × 6 = 18, so 18 tens. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: area 30 x 6
Look for: 180 − 6. Ask: "How much do you take away this time?" Model: area 30-1 x 6

responses.tip: Ask: 1 what? How big is each group?

problems.notes: Look for: 150 − 3. Ask: "What's the friendly number?" Model: area 50-1 x 3

responses.tip: Added instead of taking away. Ask: is 49 more or less than 50?

problems.notes: Look for: 500 − 10. Ask: "How many fives too many?" Model: area 100-2 x 5

responses.tip: Ask: 2 what? How big is each group?

problems.notes: Look for: 400 − 2. Ask: "Does it work with bigger numbers?" Model: area 200-1 x 2

strings.title: Double, Double Again
strings.label: Day 4
strings.group: Grade 4 · Week 2 · Multiplying by One Digit
strings.strategy: Times 4 is double, then double again; times 8 is double three times.
strings.keywords: double, times 2, times 4, times 8, ratio table
strings.connection: Builds on doubles facts. A ratio table keeps track of each double.
watchFor: Doubling only once for × 4 (4 × 12 = 24): ask "Is 4 groups the same as 2 groups?"
Doubling one more or one fewer time than needed for × 8: point to the ratio table and ask "How many groups now?"
Mistakes in doubling numbers like 35 (70) or 45 (90): ask "Double the tens, double the ones, then add."
strings.wrapUp: Ask "How can doubling help with × 4 and × 8?" Land: 4 is 2 doubled and 8 is 4 doubled, so double, double (and double again).

problems.notes: Look for: double 12. Ask: "Hold on to this." Model: ratio 1:12, 2:24
Look for: double 24. Ask: "How does the last one help?" Word choice: "4 is double 2, so I doubled 24." Model: ratio 1:12, 2:24, 4:48

responses.tip: The target strategy. Ask: why double again?
Yesterday's split. Compare.
Doubled once. Ask: is 4 groups the same as 2 groups?

problems.notes: Look for: double 48. Ask: "Can you keep doubling?" Model: ratio 1:12, 2:24, 4:48, 8:96

responses.tip: Doubled too many times. Ask: how many groups is that?

problems.notes: Look for: 70, then 140. Ask: "What's double 35?" Model: ratio 1:35, 2:70, 4:140

responses.tip: Doubled once. Ask: how many groups of 35 is 70?

problems.notes: Look for: 50, 100, 200. Ask: "How many doubles for 8?" Model: ratio 1:25, 2:50, 4:100, 8:200

responses.say: 4 quarters is a dollar, so 8 quarters is 2 dollars: 200.
responses.tip: Money connection. Name it.
Ask: did the 5 get multiplied too?

problems.notes: Look for: 250, 500. Ask: "Can you double 125?" Model: ratio 1:125, 2:250, 4:500

responses.tip: Tuesday's split. Compare.

strings.title: Choosing a Strategy
strings.label: Day 5
strings.group: Grade 4 · Week 2 · Multiplying by One Digit
strings.strategy: Look at the numbers first, then choose: times 10, split tens and ones, over and back, or double and double again.
strings.keywords: choose, friendly numbers, split, over and back, double
watchFor: Using the same strategy every time: ask "What do you notice about these numbers?"
Forgetting to take away a whole group: ask "How many groups too many?"
Not checking the size: ask "About how big should the answer be?"
strings.wrapUp: Ask "Which strategy did you choose for each, and what made you choose it?" Land: close to a ten → over and back; × 4 or × 8 → double; otherwise split tens and ones.

problems.notes: Look for: half of 10 × 18. Ask: "How is × 5 related to × 10?" Model: ratio 10:180, 5:90

responses.tip: Five is half of ten. Name it.
Ask: is the answer closer to 50 or 500?

problems.notes: Look for: 10 × 25 − 25. Ask: "Is 9 close to a friendly number?" Model: area 10-1 x 25

responses.tip: Ask: how many 25s too many?

problems.notes: Look for: double, double (52, 104), or 4 × 25 + 4. Ask: "Which strategy fits?" Model: ratio 1:26, 2:52, 4:104
Look for: 210 + 14. Ask: "How will you split 32?" Model: area 30+2 x 7

responses.tip: Ask: is the answer about 30 sevens?

problems.notes: Look for: 600 − 6. Ask: "What's friendly about 99?" Model: area 100-1 x 6

responses.tip: Ask: how many sixes too many?

problems.notes: Look for: 250 + 250 + 250, or 3 × 25 tens. Ask: "What do you know about 250?" Model: numberline +250 +250 +250
Look for: 30, 60, 120. Ask: "× 8: what can you do?" Model: ratio 1:15, 2:30, 4:60, 8:120
